content: Paratyphoid fever is a group of enteric illnesses caused by specific strains of the bacterium Salmonella paratyphi. There are three species responsible for paratyphoid fever: Salmonella paratyphi A, Salmonella paratyphi B (also known as S. schottmuelleri), and Salmonella paratyphi C (also known as S. hirschfeldii). These bacteria are transmitted through the ingestion of contaminated water or food. Typhoid fever is an acute, life-threatening febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi. Paratyphoid fever, while similar to typhoid fever, is caused by S. paratyphi A, B, or C. The clinical course of paratyphoid fever is generally milder and less severe than typhoid fever. Paratyphoid fever is caused by any of the three strains of Salmonella paratyphi: S. paratyphi A, S. schottmuelleri (S. paratyphi B), or S. hirschfeldii (S. paratyphi C). Paratyphoid fever can be differentiated from typhoid fever by its more abrupt onset, milder symptoms, and shorter duration of illness. Infections with S. paratyphi A are common in Africa and present with a clinical course similar to typhoid fever, but with more abundant and larger rose spots. S. paratyphi B is more frequently encountered in Europe, while S. paratyphi C is rare and typically seen in the Far East. Globally, there are an estimated 22 million cases of typhoid fever and 200,000 related deaths annually, along with an additional 6 million cases of paratyphoid fever. In the United States, approximately 300 cases of typhoid fever and 150 cases of paratyphoid fever are reported each year, most of which occur in recent travelers. Paratyphoid fever can affect individuals of any age, as it is transmitted through contaminated food and water. Humans are the only known reservoir for these bacteria, with no animal or environmental reservoirs identified. The disease is most commonly acquired through the consumption of water or food contaminated with the feces of an acutely infected, convalescent, or chronic asymptomatic carrier. Rarely, transmission has been documented through sexual contact, particularly among men who have sex with men. The risk of paratyphoid fever is increasing among travelers to southern and Southeast Asia, with the highest risk in southern Asia for infections that are resistant to nalidixic acid or multidrug-resistant (resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) strains. Travelers visiting friends and relatives (VFRs) are at increased risk. Although the risk of acquiring typhoid or paratyphoid fever increases with the duration of stay, infections have been reported even during visits of less than one week to endemic areas. Serious complications of paratyphoid fever typically occur after 2–3 weeks of illness and may include intestinal hemorrhage or perforation, which can be life-threatening. Death from S. paratyphi A is rare and usually associated with severe intestinal complications. With proper diagnostic testing and treatment, the mortality rate is reduced to less than 1%. On physical examination, paratyphoid fever may present with hepatosplenomegaly (enlargement of the liver and spleen). Laboratory findings show that a single blood culture is positive in only about 50% of cases. Stool cultures are generally not positive during the acute phase of the disease. Bone marrow cultures increase the diagnostic yield to approximately 80% of cases. The Widal test, an older serologic assay for detecting IgM and IgG antibodies to the O and H antigens of Salmonella, is unreliable but widely used in developing countries due to its low cost. Newer serologic assays are somewhat more sensitive and specific than the Widal test but are not widely available. Since there is no definitive serologic test for typhoid or paratyphoid fever, the diagnosis often relies on clinical judgment. S. paratyphi B is diagnosed by isolating the organism from blood or stool and demonstrating anti-BH antibodies in the Widal test. Antibodies to S. paratyphi C are not typically tested, and the diagnosis is made through blood cultures. Empiric treatment for paratyphoid fever in most parts of the world involves the use of a fluoroquinolone, most commonly ciprofloxacin. However, resistance to fluoroquinolones is highest in the Indian subcontinent and is increasing in other regions. Injectable third-generation cephalosporins are often the empiric drugs of choice when fluoroquinolone resistance is suspected. Patients treated with appropriate antibiotics may still require 3–5 days to fully defervesce, although the fever height decreases daily. Some patients may feel worse as the fever begins to subside. If fever persists beyond five days, alternative antimicrobial agents or other foci of infection should be considered. Control of the disease requires antibiotic treatment and, in some cases, vaccination as prescribed by a physician. Major treatment regimens for paratyphoid fever include ciprofloxacin for ten days, ceftriaxone or cefotaxime for 14 days, or azithromycin. S. paratyphi B responds well to chloramphenicol or co-trimoxazole. Chloramphenicol therapy is generally effective for S. paratyphi C. Primary prevention of paratyphoid fever involves educating children and adults about personal hygiene, including thorough handwashing after defecation, sexual contact, and before preparing or eating food. Proper disposal of feces is essential. Food handlers should be trained in personal hygiene before handling food, utensils, or equipment. Infected individuals should avoid food preparation. Travelers to countries with poor sanitation should receive a typhoid vaccine before departure, which protects against typhoid fever but not paratyphoid infections caused by S. paratyphi A, B, or C. Sexually active individuals should be educated about the risks of practices that allow fecal-oral contact. Owners of tropical fish should ensure meticulous cleaning of aquariums to eliminate potential S. paratyphi B organisms. Secondary prevention includes excluding symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals from work and social activities if they are food handlers, healthcare or daycare staff involved in patient or child care, children attending unsanitary daycare centers, or older children unable to maintain good personal hygiene. This exclusion remains in effect until two consecutive stool specimens from the infected individual test negative.
